chunks.text: 3 Methodology Figure 2 : Overview of MFE-MIL. Patch features e i e_{i} from a frozen encoder are mapped by a trainable two-block MLP adapter (Linear–LayerNorm–ReLU–Dropout, × 2 \times 2 ) to h i h_{i} . The adapted features feed a MIL head, trained with ℒ MIL \mathcal{L}_{\text{MIL}} , and, during training only, a reconstruction branch: features are packed in extraction order into a grid, contiguous windows are masked, and a Transformer decoder reconstructs the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized frozen embeddings e ¯ i \bar{e}_{i} of the masked patches ( ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} ; dashed arrow: reconstruction target). No patch coordinates are used, and the decoder is discarded at inference. High within-slide patch variance (staining, scanner, local texture) can overwhelm the discriminative signal, and frozen encoders further encode physical artifacts (folds, pen marks, bubbles) as distinctive, drawing attention to non-pathological regions. Rather than encoding space architecturally as prior methods do [ 11 ] , MFE-MIL shapes the feature space through the training objective: the MIL classification loss compresses within-slide variance, and a jointly optimized window-based masked-reconstruction pretext task provides an auxiliary reconstruction regularizer on the adapted features. The attention entropy in Tab. 5 shows that this compression sharpens tumour attention rather than flattening it. Overall architecture. Given a WSI bag 𝒳 = { x i } i = 1 N \mathcal{X}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , a frozen pretrained encoder f enc f_{\text{enc}} produces patch embeddings e i = f enc ​ ( x i ) e_{i}=f_{\text{enc}}(x_{i}) ; a two-layer MLP adapter g θ g_{\theta} maps these into a task-specific latent space feeding two branches: h i = g θ ​ ( e i ) ⏟ adapter , H ~ ^ = f dec ​ ( H ~ ′ , M , P ) ⏟ reconstruction (train only) , Y ^ = f class ​ ( f agg ​ ( H ) ) ⏟ MIL head .

(1) The decoder is discarded at inference, leaving only the adapter and MIL head. Task-aware MLP adapter. In the spirit of parameter-efficient fine-tuning [ 12 , 35 ] , the adapter is a two-block MLP, g θ = ϕ 2 ∘ ϕ 1 g_{\theta}=\phi_{2}\circ\phi_{1} , where each block applies a linear layer, layer normalization, ReLU, and dropout: ϕ k ​ ( x ) = Dropout 0.25 ​ ( ReLU ​ ( LN ​ ( W k ​ x + b k ) ) ) , W k ∈ ℝ D × D , \phi_{k}(x)=\text{Dropout}_{0.25}\!\bigl(\text{ReLU}\bigl(\text{LN}(W_{k}x+b_{k})\bigr)\bigr),\qquad W_{k}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{D\times D}, (2) where D D is the frozen encoder output dimension ( 384 384 , 512 512 , 1024 1024 , and 1024 1024 for ViT-S/16-SSL, CONCH, UNI, and ViT-L/16-IN21K). The adapter preserves the feature dimension ( d = D d\!=\!D ), so it is a drop-in replacement with no architectural change downstream; for UNI it adds 2.1 2.1 M parameters. The decoder reconstructs the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -normalized frozen embeddings e ¯ i = e i / ‖ e i ‖ 2 \bar{e}_{i}=e_{i}/\|e_{i}\|_{2} of the masked patches from the adapted features of the visible ones. The target is a fixed function of the frozen encoder and does not change during training, so the reconstruction loss cannot be reduced by collapsing the adapter output: if all h i h_{i} were a constant, the decoder could not recover the varying targets and ℒ rec \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}} would stay high. The adapter must therefore keep enough information to predict masked features, while the classification loss shapes the same representation toward class-discriminative directions. The reconstruction branch takes the normalized embeddings e ¯ i \bar{e}_{i} as adapter input, whereas the MIL branch takes the unnormalized e i e_{i} . Packed grid and masked reconstruction.

Given bag 𝒳 = { x i } i = 1 N \mathcal{X}=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , the frozen encoder produces embeddings e i e_{i} and the adapter produces H = [ h 1 , … , h N ] ⊤ H=[h_{1},\ldots,h_{N}]^{\top} . The reconstruction grid is built without patch coordinates: the N N adapted features are packed in tissue-extraction order into a square grid of side R = C = ⌈ N ⌉ R\!=\!C\!=\!\lceil\sqrt{N}\rceil , H ~ [ ⌊ k / C ⌋ , k mod C , : ] = h k , k = 0 , … , N − 1 , \tilde{H}\bigl[\lfloor k/C\rfloor,\;k\bmod C,\;:\bigr]=h_{k},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1, (3) giving H ~ ∈ ℝ R × C × d \tilde{H}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{R\times C\times d} (the reconstruction branch packs h ¯ k = g θ ​ ( e ¯ k ) \bar{h}_{k}=g_{\theta}(\bar{e}_{k}) in place of h k h_{k} ); the trailing R ⋅ C − N R\!\cdot\!C\!-\!N cells are zero-padded. Patches are extracted in raster order over the tissue contour, so cells that are adjacent within a row are often physically adjacent on the slide. This coordinate-free packing therefore preserves only partial locality: measured against the true patch coordinates, within-row precision is 0.89 0.89 – 0.97 0.97 across datasets and across-row precision is below 0.05 0.05 (see the supplementary material), since the correspondence breaks down across rows, at row wraps, and at irregular tissue boundaries. The pipeline uses no patch coordinates at either training or inference; we show in Sec. 4.7 that the resulting regularization does not reliably depend on the spatial arrangement of the mask. The decoder receives fixed 2D sine-cosine positional embeddings P r , c = SinCos2D ​ ( r , c ) ∈ ℝ d dec P_{r,c}=\text{SinCos2D}(r,\,c)\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{dec}}} (4) for each grid cell, where d dec = 512 d_{\text{dec}}\!=\!512 is the decoder width. Applying structured mask M ∈ { 0 , 1 } R × C M\in\{0,1\}^{R\times C} gives H ~ ′ = Mask ​ ( H ~ , M ) , H ~ ^ = f dec ​ ( H ~ ′ , M , P ) . \tilde{H}^{\prime}=\text{Mask}(\tilde{H},M),\quad\hat{\tilde{H}}=f_{\text{dec}}(\tilde{H}^{\prime},M,P).

(5) The reconstruction loss is the mean squared error between the decoder output and the normalized frozen embeddings E ¯ ∈ ℝ R × C × D \bar{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{R\times C\times D} (packed like H ~ \tilde{H} ) over the masked positions ℳ \mathcal{M} : ℒ rec = 1 | ℳ | ​ D ∑ ( i , j ) ∈ ℳ ∥ E ¯ i , j , : − H ~ ^ i , j , : ∥ 2 2 , \mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|\,D}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{M}}\bigl\|\bar{E}_{i,j,:}-\hat{\tilde{H}}_{i,j,:}\bigr\|_{2}^{2}, (6) where ℳ \mathcal{M} denotes the masked cells that hold a real patch; zero-padded cells may be masked but are excluded from ℳ \mathcal{M} , so the decoder is never asked to reconstruct absent tissue. Window-based adaptive masking. To prevent the decoder from trivially interpolating from immediately adjacent patches, we mask blocks that are contiguous in the packed grid rather than individual tokens. We define a square window of radius w w centered at grid cell ( p , q ) (p,q) : 𝒲 ⁡ ( p , q , w ) \displaystyle\mathcal{W}(p,q,w) = { ( i , j ) : | i − p | ≤ w , | j − q | ≤ w } , \displaystyle=\{(i,j):|i-p|\leq w,\;|j-q|\leq w\}, (7) | 𝒲 | = ( 2 ​ w + 1 ) 2 , \displaystyle|\mathcal{W}|=(2w+1)^{2}, and build ℳ \mathcal{M} in two phases. First, non-overlapping windows of radius w ∈ { 1 , 2 } w\in\{1,2\} (i.e., × 3 3\!\times\!3 or × 5 5\!\times\!5 blocks, chosen uniformly at random) are placed at random grid positions until they cover about 80 % 80\% of the masking budget N target = ⌊ r ⋅ R ​ C ⌋ N_{\text{target}}=\lfloor r\cdot RC\rfloor , where R ​ C RC is the number of cells of the packed grid. The remaining cells are then masked individually ( w = 0 w=0 ) to reach the budget exactly. Masking whole blocks of the packed grid makes the pretext task harder than masking single cells, and empirically gives the best AUC ( Tab. 2 ). This two-phase strategy (illustrated in the supplementary material) outperforms any fixed window size ( Tab. 2 ). We set r = 75 % r\!=\!75\% following MAE [ 13 ] . Decoder architecture.

The decoder f dec f_{\text{dec}} is a lightweight Transformer with a fixed hidden width d dec = 512 d_{\text{dec}}\!=\!512 independent of D D . A linear layer maps the D D -dimensional adapted features to d dec d_{\text{dec}} , four Transformer blocks (16 attention heads of dimension 32, feedforward → → 512 512\!\to\!2048\!\to\!512 , i.e., ratio 4) process the tokens, and a final LayerNorm and linear layer map back to D D dimensions. This amounts to about 13.7 13.7 M parameters for D = 1024 D\!=\!1024 ( 13.0 13.0 M for ViT-S and 13.1 13.1 M for CONCH). Before decoding, each masked grid cell is replaced by a learned [MASK] token to separate known from unknown positions. The 2D positional embeddings P P are added to all tokens so the decoder can use absolute grid location during reconstruction. Joint training objective. The MIL head aggregates adapted features for bag-level prediction: z = f agg ​ ( H ) , Y ^ = f class ​ ( z ) . z=f_{\text{agg}}(H),\quad\hat{Y}=f_{\text{class}}(z). The total objective balances classification and reconstruction: ℒ total = ( 1 − λ rec ) ​ ℒ MIL + λ rec ​ ℒ rec , \mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}=(1-\lambda_{\text{rec}})\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{MIL}}+\lambda_{\text{rec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{rec}}, where λ rec = 0.3 \lambda_{\text{rec}}=0.3 is chosen from { 0.1 , 0.2 , 0.3 } \{0.1,0.2,0.3\} (supplementary). Only the MLP adapter, decoder, and MIL head are updated; the foundation encoder is frozen. The MIL branch never uses decoder outputs, so discarding the decoder causes no train–test mismatch; Tab. 4 is computed on adapter outputs alone. We evaluate f agg f_{\text{agg}} as: mean/max pooling, ABMIL [ 15 ] , CLAM-SB and CLAM-MB [ 23 ] , and TransMIL [ 27 ] . The full training procedure is summarized in the supplementary material. Plug-and-play aggregator compatibility. The adapter maps each patch independently and keeps its dimension, so any aggregator that consumed { e i } \{e_{i}\} can consume { h i } \{h_{i}\} unchanged.

At inference the pipeline is encoder → frozen e i → g θ h i → f agg z → f class Y ^ \text{encoder}\xrightarrow{\text{frozen}}e_{i}\xrightarrow{g_{\theta}}h_{i}\xrightarrow{f_{\text{agg}}}z\xrightarrow{f_{\text{class}}}\hat{Y} , with no decoder, whereas coordinate-based methods such as CAMIL need explicit spatial inputs. 4 Experiments Figure 3 : ACC / F1 / AUC (%) for six MIL aggregators without (solid) and with (dashed) MFE-MIL ( UNI ). Means over 3 splits × \times 5 seeds; details in the supplementary. 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets. CAMELYON16 [ 3 ] (400 WSIs, tumour detection), CAMELYON17 [ 2 ] (500 WSIs, ITC/micro/macro grouped as positive), PANDA [ 4 ] (10,614 prostate biopsies, 6 Gleason grades, 8:1:1), TCGA-BRCA [ 30 ] (1,033 slides, IDC vs. ILC, 8:1:1). Five TCGA cohorts [ 30 ] (KIRC, KIRP, LUAD, STAD, UCEC) are used for survival. All WSIs are tiled into 256 × \times 256 patches at 20 × \times with tissue detection and patch extraction performed by AtlasPatch [ 1 ] . All splits are made at the patient (case) level, so slides from the same patient never span splits. All experiments use a 3 splits × \times 5 seeds setting, and on CAMELYON16 the official 128-slide test set is held fixed across all runs. Encoders. Pathology-pretrained UNI [ 5 ] , CONCH [ 22 ] , and ViT-S/16-SSL [ 17 ] , plus general-purpose ViT-L/16-IN21K [ 9 ] . Baselines. CAMIL, 2DMamba, and MHIM-MIL were run with their official default hyperparameters on the same split and run protocol. All methods use identical frozen features. Implementation.

Classification models are trained with Adam (lr × 10 − 4 1\!\times\!10^{-4} , no weight decay) for up to 200 epochs with early stopping on validation AUC (patience 10; macro one-vs-rest AUC for PANDA), one slide per step (batch size 1), class-balanced sampling of training slides, fp16 mixed precision, masking ratio r = 75 % r\!=\!75\% , and λ rec = 0.3 \lambda_{\text{rec}}\!=\!0.3 . Survival models use Adam (lr × 10 − 4 2\!\times\!10^{-4} , weight decay × 10 − 5 1\!\times\!10^{-5} ) with gradient accumulation over 32 slides and up to 20 epochs with early stopping on validation C-index (patience 5). No learning-rate schedule is used, and all runs use a single NVIDIA H100. Metrics. Slide-level ACC / macro-F1 / AUC (one-vs-rest for PANDA’s six grades), and C-index for survival. 4.2 Survival Prediction We first evaluate MFE-MIL on survival prediction, an established weakly-supervised WSI task typically addressed with attention-MIL or multimodal histology–genomics models [ 6 , 16 ] : the MIL head is substituted with a discrete-time hazard output over four survival-time bins, trained with the negative log-likelihood survival loss, with the adapter and reconstruction branch otherwise unchanged. Tab. 1 reports concordance index (C-index) on the five TCGA cohorts (UNI embeddings) for each aggregator with and without MFE-MIL. Among the spatially aware baselines, only 2DMamba is reported here: CAMIL and SETMIL provide no survival-prediction implementation, so they are excluded from this task. MFE-MIL improves the average C-index ( Tab. 1 , AVG column) for every one of the six aggregators tested, making it the most consistent result in this paper. Every MFE-MIL variant also exceeds the average C-index of the spatially aware 2DMamba ( 0.699 0.699 – 0.714 0.714 versus 0.695 0.695 ), without using patch coordinates. Paired t t -tests over all cohort and aggregator pairs confirm the overall improvement is statistically significant ( p < 0.05 p<0.05 ).

The largest gains are on UCEC and KIRP, two cohorts with diffuse prognostic signals; STAD gains are small or negative for high-baseline aggregators, while MAX, with the lowest STAD baseline, gains 0.081 0.081 . However, MAX’s baseline C-index is near-chance on KIRP, LUAD and STAD, so its large gains mainly reflect fixing a weak baseline; the smaller, consistent gains on ABMIL, CLAM-MB, and CLAM-SB are the more informative signal. On KIRC most aggregators plateau; the exceptions are MAX and CLAM-MB, which rise 0.047 0.047 and 0.011 0.011 , and TransMIL, which drops 0.015 0.015 , likely because compressing within-slide variance reduces the per-patch diversity that its long-range self-attention relies on. The CONCH counterpart and full numerical results for all four encoders are in the supplementary (SETMIL [ 39 ] is omitted, as it failed to converge on CAMELYON16/17 with these encoders).

MFE-MIL improves ACC and F1 for every aggregator under the UNI and CONCH encoders and in nearly all ViT-L/ViT-S settings, with gains largest where the baseline is weakest; paired t t -tests over 15 runs are significant on CAMELYON16, CAMELYON17, and PANDA ( p < 0.05 p<0.05 ) but not on TCGA-BRCA ( p = 0.19 p=0.19 ). Against spatially aware baselines, MFE-MIL beats CAMIL on all four datasets without coordinate graphs at inference, and by AUC the best MFE variant leads 2DMamba on all but TCGA-BRCA (within one std); MFE-ABMIL beats MHIM-MIL on ACC and F1 across all datasets and both encoders, and on AUC for two of four datasets under each encoder. AUC regressions are rare and small (at most 0.8 0.8 points), mostly on near-ceiling TCGA-BRCA, where UNI baseline AUC is already 96.3 96.3 – 98.0 % 98.0\% for every aggregator, leaving too little headroom for a gain to reach significance. On the general-purpose ViT-L/16-IN21K and the smaller pathology-pretrained ViT-S/16-SSL encoders (full results in the supplementary), MFE-MIL’s gains are larger than on UNI and CONCH (e.g., ViT-L ABMIL CAMELYON17 AUC → 82.8 78.7\!\to\!82.8 ), consistent with weaker features carrying more within-slide variance to suppress. MFE-MIL also exceeds the recent ACMIL [ 38 ] aggregator on AUC across all four datasets (supplementary). The supplementary UNI table isolates the reconstruction branch using a classification-only adapter (frozen → \to adapter → \to +MFE). For ABMIL, CLAM-MB, and CLAM-SB, the adapter alone is inconsistent relative to frozen features, while adding reconstruction improves AUC in every case, most notably on CAMELYON16/17 and more modestly on near-saturated PANDA; for MAX it is slightly lower on CAMELYON16/17 ( → 98.31 98.62\!\to\!98.31 , → 95.31 95.53\!\to\!95.31 ). By contrast, CAMIL needs 14.60 14.60 GB and 0.353 0.353 s for graph construction, and 2DMamba 4.60 4.60 GB and 0.082 0.082 s. Training adds the reconstruction decoder ( 13.7 13.7 M parameters), which raises per-epoch time and peak training memory by ∼ 6 × {\sim}6\times on CAMELYON16 and end-to-end training time by ∼ 21 × {\sim}21\times ; this is a one-time cost, as the decoder is discarded at inference. 4.5 Ablation Studies All ablations use PANDA with UNI embeddings. Reported AUC values use three pre-defined splits × \times 5 seeds. Adapter depth and masking strategy. Capacity alone does not explain the gain ( Tab. 2 , top block): MIL-only AUC is non-monotonic in depth and never reaches depth-2 MFE-MIL’s performance; adding reconstruction improves every depth, and depth-2 MFE-MIL (our full model) is best overall, though CLAM-SB peaks at depth-1, likely because its single attention branch saturates at lower adapter capacity while deeper adapters slightly overfit its instance loss. Masking granularity also matters for AUC ( Tab. 2 , bottom block): random single-token and × 3 3\!\times\!3 masking stall at 93.56 93.56 avg. AUC, a fixed × 5 5\!\times\!5 window reaches 93.88 93.88 , and adaptive multi-scale window masking is best, preventing the decoder from exploiting any single predictable block size. A per-slide z-score normalization control does not replicate the learned adapter: it leaves attention entropy indistinguishable from frozen features ( 0.982 0.982 versus 0.985 0.985 ) and makes the coherence ratio numerically unstable (supplementary). 4.6 Qualitative Evaluation WSI ABMIL MFE-ABMIL CAM16 LUAD UCEC Figure 5 : ABMIL attention without and with MFE-MIL (UNI; blue = low, red = high). On CAMELYON16 the baseline attends to a tissue-fold artifact; MFE-MIL attends to the tumour. TCGA-LUAD and UCEC are where the pathologist saw the clearest improvement; all cohorts (including exceptions) and CLAM heads are in the supplementary. For the qualitative study, a single board-certified pathologist (unblinded, using a qualitative rubric; not a quantitative validation) reviewed 10 randomly selected WSIs from each of the five TCGA survival cohorts (KIRC, KIRP, LUAD, STAD, UCEC) together with their attention maps; Fig. 5 shows examples (all cohorts and aggregators in the supplementary).

The pathologist assessed how well attention focused on the lesion, whether the high-attention areas within the lesion correlated with known pathology features, and how much attention fell on background regions of low pathological value. Attention maps varied with both task and dataset. Overall, MFE-MIL placed higher attention on lesion regions and showed better visual agreement with pathologist-identified tissue features. This was most evident on the TCGA-LUAD and UCEC cohorts; KIRC and STAD were the exceptions, while on KIRP the two models produced similar maps. Quantitative attention localization. We further score attention against the pixel-level tumour annotations on the CAMELYON16 test set ( Tab. 3 ). Treating each patch’s attention weight as a tumour score, MFE-MIL improves localization AUROC for all three aggregators and pointing-game accuracy for ABMIL and CLAM-MB (unchanged for CLAM-SB), quantifying the improved tumour localization seen in Fig. 5 . A paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the slides with a defined patch-level AUROC confirms the gain is significant for ABMIL ( p = × 10 − 5 p\!=\!4.1\!\times\!10^{-5} ) and CLAM-SB ( p = 0.003 p\!=\!0.003 ); the smaller CLAM-MB gain does not reach significance ( p = 0.056 p\!=\!0.056 ). This pattern mirrors the larger gains for weaker baselines: the gain is largest and most reliable for the weakest-localizing baseline (ABMIL) and smallest and not significant for the best-localizing one (CLAM-MB), consistent with the variance-suppression mechanism. Top-50 attention mass is essentially unchanged, indicating that MFE-MIL improves the ranking of tumour patches rather than concentrating additional total attention mass on them, consistent with the class-selective entropy sharpening in Tab. 5 . A supplementary t-SNE figure further shows that MFE-MIL induces class-separable structure in the latent space.

Unlike the coordinate-free training grid, this analysis takes neighbours directly from the pixel coordinates stored during patch extraction (patch step 256 256 ), so the neighbour sets below are genuinely spatial. For each patch we compare cosine similarity to its 4-connected spatial neighbours (adj) against similarity to 2000 randomly sampled distant patches (rand); the gap adj − - rand compares adjacent with random-pair similarity. Together with the coherence ratio, three further metrics are reported: normalised ABMIL attention entropy ( Tab. 5 ), plus top- k k attention coherence and effective rank of the adapter output matrix (both in the supplementary). All four agree that classification drives most of the compression; differences between masking variants are small. Frozen UNI features start at a spatial coherence ratio of 1.952 × 1.952\times . We contrast three conditions all with 2-layer MLP: Baseline (classification-only adapter; “MIL, 2” in Tab. 2 ), Rand MFE (single-token random masking; “Single-token”), and Win MFE (window masking, our full model; “Window (ours)”); results are in Tab. 4 .

All three conditions dramatically compress within-slide variance. The ratio drops from 1.952 × 1.952\times to 1.07 1.07 – 1.10 × 1.10\times regardless of masking strategy, which confirms that classification alone is the dominant driver of this semantic compression, i.e., the reduction of within-slide feature variance. Across all masking variants the coherence gap falls in a narrow band with no reliable ordering by spatial arrangement or grouping: shuffling the packed order, using true-coordinate windows, 1D contiguous masks, distance-matched scattered groups, and single-token random masking all give comparable gaps under matched controls (supplementary), given the large split-to-split variation. Win MFE’s larger CAMELYON16 gap comes mainly from lower random-pair similarity ( 0.874 0.874 versus 0.904 0.904 for Baseline), while adjacent-pair similarity also drops ( 0.958 0.958 versus 0.968 0.968 ), so it reflects greater global dispersion rather than closer neighbours. The gap therefore reflects the masked-reconstruction objective acting as a representation regularizer, rather than preservation of tissue-level spatial neighbourhoods. The larger window-versus-single-token gap on CAMELYON16 ( Tab. 4 ) is within this variation and is not reproduced on PANDA in the matched controls (0.058 versus 0.057; supplementary); in all cases the effect is modest and dataset-dependent, clearer on CAMELYON16 than on PANDA, where the gap barely moves even though downstream AUC still improves. The compression direction generalises across encoders: CONCH features show the same overall adj/rand ratio reduction as UNI, with benign tissue (Grade 0) compressing the most (supplementary), supporting the encoder-agnostic claim. 4.1 Experimental Setup Datasets. CAMELYON16 [ 3 ] (400 WSIs, tumour detection), CAMELYON17 [ 2 ] (500 WSIs, ITC/micro/macro grouped as positive), PANDA [ 4 ] (10,614 prostate biopsies, 6 Gleason grades, 8:1:1), TCGA-BRCA [ 30 ] (1,033 slides, IDC vs. ILC, 8:1:1). Five TCGA cohorts [ 30 ] (KIRC, KIRP, LUAD, STAD, UCEC) are used for survival. All WSIs are tiled into 256 × \times 256 patches at 20 × \times with tissue detection and patch extraction performed by AtlasPatch [ 1 ] . All splits are made at the patient (case) level, so slides from the same patient never span splits. All experiments use a 3 splits × \times 5 seeds setting, and on CAMELYON16 the official 128-slide test set is held fixed across all runs. Encoders. Pathology-pretrained UNI [ 5 ] , CONCH [ 22 ] , and ViT-S/16-SSL [ 17 ] , plus general-purpose ViT-L/16-IN21K [ 9 ] . Baselines. CAMIL, 2DMamba, and MHIM-MIL were run with their official default hyperparameters on the same split and run protocol. All methods use identical frozen features. Implementation.

Classification models are trained with Adam (lr × 10 − 4 1\!\times\!10^{-4} , no weight decay) for up to 200 epochs with early stopping on validation AUC (patience 10; macro one-vs-rest AUC for PANDA), one slide per step (batch size 1), class-balanced sampling of training slides, fp16 mixed precision, masking ratio r = 75 % r\!=\!75\% , and λ rec = 0.3 \lambda_{\text{rec}}\!=\!0.3 . Survival models use Adam (lr × 10 − 4 2\!\times\!10^{-4} , weight decay × 10 − 5 1\!\times\!10^{-5} ) with gradient accumulation over 32 slides and up to 20 epochs with early stopping on validation C-index (patience 5). No learning-rate schedule is used, and all runs use a single NVIDIA H100. Metrics. Slide-level ACC / macro-F1 / AUC (one-vs-rest for PANDA’s six grades), and C-index for survival. 4.3 Classification Results Fig. 3 reports per-aggregator ACC/F1/AUC on all four datasets with UNI embeddings, and Fig. 4 shows the AUC of all six aggregators next to the spatially aware baselines CAMIL [ 11 ] and 2DMamba [ 37 ] and the masking-based MHIM-MIL [ 29 ] . The CONCH counterpart and full numerical results for all four encoders are in the supplementary (SETMIL [ 39 ] is omitted, as it failed to converge on CAMELYON16/17 with these encoders). MFE-MIL improves ACC and F1 for every aggregator under the UNI and CONCH encoders and in nearly all ViT-L/ViT-S settings, with gains largest where the baseline is weakest; paired t t -tests over 15 runs are significant on CAMELYON16, CAMELYON17, and PANDA ( p < 0.05 p<0.05 ) but not on TCGA-BRCA ( p = 0.19 p=0.19 ). Against spatially aware baselines, MFE-MIL beats CAMIL on all four datasets without coordinate graphs at inference, and by AUC the best MFE variant leads 2DMamba on all but TCGA-BRCA (within one std); MFE-ABMIL beats MHIM-MIL on ACC and F1 across all datasets and both encoders, and on AUC for two of four datasets under each encoder.

AUC regressions are rare and small (at most 0.8 0.8 points), mostly on near-ceiling TCGA-BRCA, where UNI baseline AUC is already 96.3 96.3 – 98.0 % 98.0\% for every aggregator, leaving too little headroom for a gain to reach significance. On the general-purpose ViT-L/16-IN21K and the smaller pathology-pretrained ViT-S/16-SSL encoders (full results in the supplementary), MFE-MIL’s gains are larger than on UNI and CONCH (e.g., ViT-L ABMIL CAMELYON17 AUC → 82.8 78.7\!\to\!82.8 ), consistent with weaker features carrying more within-slide variance to suppress. MFE-MIL also exceeds the recent ACMIL [ 38 ] aggregator on AUC across all four datasets (supplementary). The supplementary UNI table isolates the reconstruction branch using a classification-only adapter (frozen → \to adapter → \to +MFE). For ABMIL, CLAM-MB, and CLAM-SB, the adapter alone is inconsistent relative to frozen features, while adding reconstruction improves AUC in every case, most notably on CAMELYON16/17 and more modestly on near-saturated PANDA; for MAX it is slightly lower on CAMELYON16/17 ( → 98.31 98.62\!\to\!98.31 , → 95.31 95.53\!\to\!95.31 ). On CAMELYON16 the baseline attends to a tissue-fold artifact; MFE-MIL attends to the tumour. TCGA-LUAD and UCEC are where the pathologist saw the clearest improvement; all cohorts (including exceptions) and CLAM heads are in the supplementary. For the qualitative study, a single board-certified pathologist (unblinded, using a qualitative rubric; not a quantitative validation) reviewed 10 randomly selected WSIs from each of the five TCGA survival cohorts (KIRC, KIRP, LUAD, STAD, UCEC) together with their attention maps; Fig. 5 shows examples (all cohorts and aggregators in the supplementary). The pathologist assessed how well attention focused on the lesion, whether the high-attention areas within the lesion correlated with known pathology features, and how much attention fell on background regions of low pathological value. Attention maps varied with both task and dataset. Overall, MFE-MIL placed higher attention on lesion regions and showed better visual agreement with pathologist-identified tissue features. This was most evident on the TCGA-LUAD and UCEC cohorts; KIRC and STAD were the exceptions, while on KIRP the two models produced similar maps. Quantitative attention localization. We further score attention against the pixel-level tumour annotations on the CAMELYON16 test set ( Tab. 3 ). Treating each patch’s attention weight as a tumour score, MFE-MIL improves localization AUROC for all three aggregators and pointing-game accuracy for ABMIL and CLAM-MB (unchanged for CLAM-SB), quantifying the improved tumour localization seen in Fig. 5 .

A paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test over the slides with a defined patch-level AUROC confirms the gain is significant for ABMIL ( p = × 10 − 5 p\!=\!4.1\!\times\!10^{-5} ) and CLAM-SB ( p = 0.003 p\!=\!0.003 ); the smaller CLAM-MB gain does not reach significance ( p = 0.056 p\!=\!0.056 ). This pattern mirrors the larger gains for weaker baselines: the gain is largest and most reliable for the weakest-localizing baseline (ABMIL) and smallest and not significant for the best-localizing one (CLAM-MB), consistent with the variance-suppression mechanism. Top-50 attention mass is essentially unchanged, indicating that MFE-MIL improves the ranking of tumour patches rather than concentrating additional total attention mass on them, consistent with the class-selective entropy sharpening in Tab. 5 . A supplementary t-SNE figure further shows that MFE-MIL induces class-separable structure in the latent space. The classification signal compresses within-slide patch variance; window-based masked reconstruction then further regularizes the adapted features.

Across CAMELYON16/17, PANDA, and TCGA-BRCA it improves ACC/F1 in nearly all settings, outperforms CAMIL without using coordinate graphs at inference, and achieves higher AUC than 2DMamba on three of four datasets (UNI). On five TCGA survival cohorts it improves the average C-index for every aggregator tested. Coherence, attention-entropy, and effective-rank analyses indicate that classification drives most of the compression, with reconstruction adding a modest regularizing effect. Limitations and ethical considerations are discussed in the supplementary.
